coverage_notes: The list held one file (a4etJo2_x7Y.txt, 3590 lines). I read all of it in chunks: all 500 saved top-level threads plus their replies. YouTube reported 3354 comments, so the 500 saved threads are a subset (the file says top-level threads saved: 500). Gap lists logins_passwords and paying_for_tools are empty: no commenter mentions shared passwords, logins, apps, or paying for any caregiving tool or software. tools_used_today is thin: only delivery services, paper boxes of records, shift schedules and a government care package appear; no one names a calendar, spreadsheet, group chat or app. No commenter says the care recipient does not want or need technology specifically (refusal is about help, strangers and moving, not tech).

videos.title: The Brutal Reality about Caring for Elderly Parents No one Talks About
videos.how_counted: Approximate. Counted by hand while reading, top-level threads and replies together, where the writer describes their own caregiving or their own family's care. A single comment can count under several themes, so counts add up to more than 330. Praise, prayers, advice to others, ads, and statements about the commenter's own future old age were not counted as own-situation (those with plans for their own old age are counted under T14).
videos.audience_note: The video is a blunt 'brutal reality' talk by a creator who worked with geriatric patients. It attracts people who are exhausted, resentful or grieving, many of them long-term or sole caregivers of a parent with dementia, aged roughly 45 to 75, many female and many nurses or care workers. It also draws older adults vowing not to burden their children, and a smaller group who say caregiving was a blessing with no regrets. Commenters who care for someone they love without strain are under-represented, so the picture over-weights burnout, guilt and sibling conflict and under-weights logistics. Many commenters are outside the US (UK, Canada, Australia, Ireland, NZ, India), which is noted where it matters.

new_themes.name: Caregiving continues after placement in a facility
new_themes.description: Commenters say moving a parent to assisted living, memory care or a nursing home does not end the workload: visiting, supply runs, appointments, monitoring care quality, phone calls, and the facility contacting the family often. Often paired with guilt.

example.quote: And even with assisted living you still have to be present and involved, do supply runs, etc.

new_themes.name: Inheritance and money disputes with siblings, and defending against accusations
new_themes.description: The caregiving sibling reports other siblings staying away but appearing at estate time, accusing them of taking money, or trying to control spending. Some keep records or video as protection. Overlaps T3 and T6 but is a distinct, recurring pattern.

example.quote: So I've had to cover myself with audit trails of all expenses,

new_themes.name: Caregiver fear of own old age and wish not to burden children
new_themes.description: Many caregivers say the experience made them write down instructions, vow never to put their own children through it, or fear no one will care for them (no children, only child, poor).

example.quote: which prompted me to draw up a living, trust, specifying that my children are to hire help and or put me in a facility if/when I can’t take care of myself

new_themes.name: Not being understood or valued by others
new_themes.description: Caregivers describe friends, neighbors and family who minimise the work (called unemployed, said to be on a vacation), give advice without helping, or drift away. Caregiving feels invisible and unpaid.

example.quote: I was told that I had enjoyed a 10 year vacation, cost free…

new_themes.name: Physical strain and injury of hands-on care
new_themes.description: Lifting, getting a parent up from a fall, bathing and toileting cause back injuries and falls for the caregiver, often an older adult themselves. Some also say intimate personal care is distressing between parent and child.

example.quote: I can’t get him up from a fall, I’m 4ft 10, and 78lbs.

new_themes.name: Cleaning out and repairing a parent's home (hoarding, deferred maintenance)
new_themes.description: Caregivers spend money and labour on clearing hoarded houses and doing repairs, often needed to sell the house to pay for care.

example.quote: My husband and I have worked ourselves to death cleaning her hoarder house and getting repairs done.

caveats: One video only, so this is one audience, not a sample of caregivers. The video title and creator frame caregiving as brutal, so comments skew toward burnout, resentment and guilt; relief and positive experiences also appear but less often. Many commenters are outside the US, so cost and benefit comments (Medicaid versus UK, Canada, Australia, Ireland) mix systems; US-specific mentions are Medicaid, Medicare, look-back periods and long-term care insurance. Many comment authors are past caregivers (recipient has died), so some problems are recalled, not current. Counts are approximate hand tallies, one comment can count under several themes, and replies by other commenters were counted when the writer described their own situation. Comments are unverified and anonymous. The video creator is a non-clinical channel owner; creator replies were not counted. Some comments are ads (comment 175) or generic praise and were excluded. Counts for T14 include mentions of end-of-life wishes, planning for own old age and dying before the parent. Several comments mention suicide or euthanasia (own or a parent's); these were not quoted except through neutral themes. Quotes were copied from the file text; a few contain the original typos and spacing.
